title: dawn-jotter-context-compression-experiments
content:
Quick brain-dump: morning run-through of papers and first-pass ideas for experiments that might reduce token cost in long-context request patterns while keeping user-visible quality. Not formal — notes to self + things to try/measure.

Why this?
- We get a lot of long-session traffic (chatbots, notebooks). Prefix reuse is high but naive caching evicts too aggressively for diverse user sequences.
- Need practical, low-risk heuristics that can be implemented in runtime without major architecture rewrites.

High-level hypothesis
- A lightweight summarizer+anchor approach ("rolling-summarizer") that compacts low-salience prefix KV into a small summary embedding + a short replayable token prefix can preserve retrieval-quality signals for many downstream prompts while reducing total KV size and CPU/GPU memory pressure.
- Combine with entropy-based eviction (keep entries with high surprise for the distribution of next-token logits) -> better tradeoff than LRU.

Notes from recent reads (scattered):
- "Contextual Compression" style papers (arXiv:2103.xxxx) argue for offloading old context to compressed representations; implementation gaps remain around reconstruction cost for autoregressive decoding.
- "Sparse KV" and "shard-aware eviction" (ICML/NeurIPS work) suggest heterogenous retention windows per document type — worthwhile to try per-route configs.
- Practical ops threads: slack thread #kv-cache-ops — monitor stall scenarios when eviction coincides with heavy batching.

Toy experiment ideas (1-2 day proofs):
1) Rolling-summarizer prototype (Py):
   - Keep standard KV for recent N tokens (e.g., last 1k). For older ranges, run a cheap summarizer heuristic (n-gram compression + strip stopwords) to produce a summary token sequence of <= 64 tokens and an embedding. Store summary as a "mini-KV" entry with metadata: original-span, last-used, surprise-score.
   - At decode time, when cache lookup includes mini-KVs, inject summary tokens as soft prefix (prepend to input) and, optionally, bias logits by a scaled dot-product of summary-embedding vs current query embedding (cheap).
   - Measure end-to-end latency delta, per-token cost reduction, and response-quality on a small prompt set (10 canonical chat sessions).

2) Entropy-anchored eviction policy:
   - Compute per-KV chunk entropy: sample a few next-token predictions conditioned on chunk (or reuse stored logits snapshot). Chunks with low entropy + low recency -> compress/evict first. Chunks with high entropy and moderate recency kept.
   - Compare to LRU baseline on synthetic replayed traffic. Metric: mean rank drop on held-out retrieval-of-pertinent-span tasks.

3) Patchwork stitching for long docs:
   - For very long documents ( > 20k tokens) store dense anchors every M tokens plus a sparse pointer table. When query references a region, expand anchors adjacent to the referenced span rather than loading full contiguous KV.
   - Use cheap lexical overlap to decide which anchors to stitch.

Eval plan (cheap, prioritized):
- Small traffic replay: 500 sessions sampled from last-week logs (anonymized) — run baseline (no compression), mini-KV, entropy-evict, rolling-summarizer. Collect: avg tokens served, avg GPU KB in use, tail latency (95/99), and human-rated quality on 50 sessions (pairwise).
- Synthetic stress: adversarially interleave many short sessions to see if mini-KV improves cache pressure and batching throughput.
- Safety / correctness checks: ensure summaries don't remove safety-critical instructions (detective: if user prompt contains "do not summarize" or structured tool call signature -> bypass compression).

Open questions / risks
- How to set summary length heuristics for multilingual data? Some languages compress poorly with simple n-gram heuristics. Maybe use byte-level sampling or a tiny summarizer model (cost tradeoff).
- Embedding-biasing at decode time may add additional compute; need to ensure it's cheaper than the memory savings.
- Instrumentation: what logs do we need to debug quality regressions? Need per-request diff traces showing which KV segments contributed.

Implementation notes / sketch code (pseudocode):
- store_mini_kv(span_tokens):
    if len(span_tokens) <= 64: store normal kv
    else:
      summary_tokens = cheap_summarize(span_tokens, budget=64)
      summary_embedding = embed(summary_tokens)
      metadata = {"orig_len": len(span_tokens), "last_used": now(), "surprise": estimate_surprise(span_tokens)}
      store({"type":"mini-kv", "tokens": summary_tokens, "emb": summary_embedding, "meta": metadata})

- decode_with_mini_kv(query):
    hits = lookup_kv(query)
    mini_hits = filter(hits, type==mini-kv)
    if mini_hits:
      prefix = concat(mini_hits.tokens)
      query2 = prefix + query
      logits = model_forward(query2)
      # optional: bias via emb similarity
    else:
      logits = model_forward(query)
    return sample(logits)

Benchmarks to capture (initial):
- tokens/sec decode (w/ and w/o mini-kv)
- memory footprint (GPU + NVMe)
- quality delta (automatic metric like ROUGE-1 and human A/B)
- regression examples (store a tiny dataset of failure cases)

Short to-do list (this sprint):
- [ ] implement cheap_summarize (start with tf-idf top-k sentence extraction) — Kevin (2d)
- [ ] build playback harness with 500 anonymized sessions — Owen (1d)
- [ ] instrumentation hook for per-kv contribution tracing — Maya (2d)
- [ ] prototype entropy scoring function and compare with LRU (local run) — Kevin (1d)
- [ ] sanity check: ensure mini-kv not used for tool-invocation prompts — default rule set — Maya (0.5d)

Notes to self: keep the first iteration simple and observable. If we get promising numbers, we can iterate on a small learned summarizer (distilled) that runs on CPU before moving to GPU-offload. Track everything under GH PR: kv-experiments/rolling-mini-kv.

References & scratch links:
- arXiv:2103.xxxx contextual compression (note: replace with exact id when drafting paper summary)
- GitHub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-experiments (proto branch: rolling-mini-kv)
- Slack: #kv-cache-ops; pinned discussion Feb 2026 about eviction tail spikes
- Confluence draft: Rolling KV Compression (draft) — Confluence id in linked_artifacts

Final quick thoughts: keep config per-route. Mobile/low-latency routes probably should not compress; long-session analytics routes should. This is an ops-first feature: incremental rollout, metric gates, regression alarms.
